Cloud security operations must process high-volume, rapidly changing telemetry within short response windows while preserving governance and accountability, yet SOCs remain constrained by alert fatigue, high false-positive rates, analyst overload, staffing shortages, fragmented tooling, and slow incident handling (Abstract, p. 1; §4.3, p. 10). The literature on cloud defense, SOC modernization, RAG, and Agentic AI is fragmented, with few studies integrating governance, detection, incident response, and agentic orchestration into a cloud-centric synthesis (§1, p. 2; §4.1, p. 8). Agentic systems additionally introduce a new attack surface: untrusted telemetry, retrieved documents, and tool responses can carry direct/indirect prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, unauthorized tool use, and cross-tenant leakage (§1, p. 2; §4.7, p. 12).

A two-part contribution: (a) a focused systematic review of 33 studies (23-study legacy corpus + 10 quality-appraised Scopus additions) answering RQ1-RQ5 (§2, p. 3; §3.1, pp. 3-4); and (b) a secure Agentic AI-driven SOCaaS conceptual framework with six core layers — multi-source telemetry ingestion, automated triage/enrichment, retrieval and context (RAG over playbooks, MITRE ATT&CK, cloud policies), agentic reasoning and orchestration, governance and human oversight, and response execution with audit — plus a cross-cutting security and trust-enforcement plane (§5.4, Fig. 4, p. 18; §5.4.1, pp. 18-19). The agentic layer performs goal-directed multistep reasoning, task decomposition, tool coordination, and response recommendation, but is explicitly bounded: model output is a recommendation, not an authorization; a deterministic policy gate outside the LLM decides deny/auto-execute/escalate, and high-impact actions require human approval (§5.1, p. 16; §5.4.5-5.4.6, pp. 19-20). Nine design principles cover cloud awareness, context-rich decision support, bounded orchestration, human oversight, auditability, modularity, adversarially robust context handling, least-privilege policy-mediated execution, and tenant isolation (§5.3, pp. 17-18); Table 4 maps six adversarial threats (prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, tool misuse, cross-tenant leakage, audit manipulation) to architectural controls (p. 19).

Two-phase focused SLR with qualitative thematic synthesis (no meta-analysis due to heterogeneity): Phase 1 legacy corpus of 23 studies (IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar); Phase 2 reproducible Scopus update reported per PRISMA 2020 — 2181 records, 70 duplicates removed, 2111 screened, 65 sought, 55 not retrieved, 10 full texts assessed and all 10 included (§3.1-3.4, pp. 3-5; Fig. 1, p. 5); protocol not prospectively registered (§3.1, p. 4); full-text quality appraisal on five 0-2 criteria with a 7/10 inclusion threshold (§3.5, p. 6). The framework is then evaluated by four seeded (seed 42), openly released component-level simulations on deliberately imperfect synthetic data (3% label noise, distractor terms, logging failures): (1) Random Forest triage on 20,000 synthetic events; (2) TF-IDF lexical retrieval over 12 playbooks and 60 paraphrased incident queries; (3) discrete-event simulation of 2000 incidents, 6 analysts, comparing manual vs. narrow-AI vs. agentic+governance operating models; (4) 1000 Monte Carlo runs of the six-step privilege-escalation workflow for audit completeness (§6.1-6.5, pp. 22-28; code on GitHub/Zenodo, Data Availability, p. 32).

Not demonstrated empirically — no real-world comparison against a concrete deployed baseline is executed; all response-time figures are outputs of a seeded discrete-event simulation under declared synthetic assumptions, which the authors frame as "internal feasibility rather than production efficacy" (Abstract, p. 1; §6, p. 22; §6.7, p. 29). Within the simulation (2000 incidents, 6 analysts, 12 incidents/hour): mean time to triage drops from 20.1 min (modeled manual SOC) and 7.1 min (narrow-AI) to 2.1 min in the governed agentic model, and mean time to respond from 59.5 and 23.4 min to 8.8 min — a 6.8-fold reduction vs. the modeled manual baseline — with 90th-percentile response at 16.5 vs. 101.8 min, analyst touches per incident 0.32 vs. 3.50, and 67.9% of actions auto-executed (§6.4, Table 8, pp. 25-26). Under rising load (6→26 incidents/hour) the agentic model stays flat at ~8.5-8.6 min while the manual model saturates beyond ~14/hour (up to >1655 min) and narrow-AI beyond ~22/hour (256.0 min) (Fig. 8b, p. 26). Threshold sensitivity shows near-total automation gains only ~3.3 min (9.9→6.6 min) while high-impact auto-execution rises from 0% to 74.15% (Table 9, Fig. 9, pp. 26-27). The paper uses "mean time to triage/respond", not MTTD/MTTR nomenclature, and threats-to-validity explicitly note that service times and risk-score quality are modeling assumptions, not measurements from a deployed SOC (§6.6, p. 28).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: The review organizes the field into three maturity levels — narrow AI detection/triage, LLM/RAG contextual support, and semi-autonomous agentic orchestration — finding the agentic level most ambitious but least validated (§4.9, Fig. 3, pp. 12-13; Table 3, p. 14). It concludes the literature favors bounded, semi-autonomous operation with human authority over full autonomy (§4.5, p. 11; §4.11, p. 16). For agent security it synthesizes benchmark/attack/defense work (AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench, MELON, AgentVigil, Prompt Infection, adaptive attacks) showing instructions propagate between agents and static defenses remain vulnerable, deriving four architectural requirements: separate instructions from data, provenance-aware retrieval from controlled sources, restricted tool access, and authorization outside the language model (§4.7, p. 12). Simulation evidence quantifies agentic design trade-offs: conservative triage gating cuts alert volume 59.5% with 4.81% threat leakage (Table 6, p. 24); retrieval grounding raises top-1 playbook mapping from 0.317 to 0.850 (Table 7, pp. 24-25); the governance threshold behaves as an organizational risk-appetite parameter with a sharply asymmetric speed-control curve (Table 9, p. 27); and audit logging costs only 1.79% mean overhead with 95.5% complete six-step evidence chains (Table 10, p. 28).

Review limitations: intermediate counts of the 23-study legacy phase were not preserved; 55 of 65 Scopus reports could not be retrieved (possible underrepresentation of subscription-only research); Web of Science was not searched; six legacy sources (18.2% of corpus) remain preprints; no quantitative meta-analysis was possible (§7, pp. 29-30; §3.2, p. 4). Validation limitations: the simulations establish internal feasibility only — Experiment 1 evaluates conventional ML (Random Forest), not generative agentic reasoning; Experiment 2 uses a TF-IDF lexical baseline, not dense RAG; Experiments 3-4 rest on assumed distributions; the queueing model omits LLM inference variation, hallucination loops, tool failures, and human factors; and no experiment tests prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, cross-tenant leakage, or audit tampering — the security plane "remains an architectural requirement until it is implemented and adversarially tested" (§6.6, p. 28; §7, pp. 29-30). Future work: broader database coverage, working prototypes tested in real cloud incident-response settings, comparative evaluation of narrow AI vs. LLM vs. RAG vs. agentic orchestration, policy engineering for approval thresholds and compliance-aware orchestration, and human-factors studies on trust calibration and workload (§7, p. 30).

Direct topical match: the paper designs an Agentic AI orchestration layer for cloud SOC incident response whose declared purpose is faster triage and response under governance — precisely the copilot-reduces-MTTD/MTTR territory of the thesis — and it is one of the few studies that explicitly quantifies (albeit in simulation) the triage-time and response-time deltas between manual, narrow-AI, and governed agentic operating models, including a load-scaling analysis explaining *why* agentic orchestration prevents MTTR saturation (analyst-queue arrival-rate reduction) (§6.4, pp. 25-26). Its six-layer architecture, nine design principles, bounded-autonomy governance gate, and threat-to-control mapping provide a reusable architectural vocabulary for the thesis framework chapter, and its three-level maturity model situates copilot approaches within the literature (§4.9, pp. 12-13; §5.3-5.4, pp. 17-20). Inclusion with caveat: the evidence is synthetic component-level simulation of a conceptual framework — no deployed agent, no real incident data, no empirical MTTD/MTTR measurement — so its numbers inform hypothesis formation and experiment design, not effect-size claims (§6.6-6.7, pp. 28-29).

High - the study sits squarely on the thesis intersection (Agentic AI copilot/orchestrator optimizing incident response time in cloud SOCs) and contributes both an SLR-grounded architecture and simulated triage/response-time comparisons across operating models. The caveat is evidentiary, not topical: all MTTD/MTTR-like gains are synthetic simulation results of a conceptual framework, to be cited as feasibility evidence only.
